newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel hits back for Katyusha attacks.
newsitem.headline: Israel hits back for Katyusha attacks.

text.p: Israeli planes unleashed rockets at targets south of Beirut on Friday just hours after Katyusha rockets fired from Lebanon hit northern Israel, the Israeli army said.
The United States condemned the cross-border attacks and urged the sides to stop the violence. Since Monday 13 people have died in the fighting.
"We've been in contact with all the parties directly to urge maximum restraint," State Department spokesman James Rubin said.
One Israeli woman was slightly injured in the Katyusha attack, which damaged a synagogue in the town of Kiryat Shmona where worshippers had gathered for morning prayers, the army said.
It was the first time Katyushas had hit the town in more than 15 months since Israel and pro-Iranian Hizbollah guerrillas undertook not to fire on civilian targets.
The understanding was part of a 1996 ceasefire that ended a 17-day Israeli onslaught mounted to protect northern towns in which about 200 people, mainly Lebanese civilians, were killed.

Israel said its planes had attacked targets in the Na'ameh hills north of its 15 km (9-mile) occupation strip inside Lebanon. It said the pilots "reported hitting their targets and all planes returned home safely".
Lebanese officials said two rockets were fired into the hills some 15 km south of Beirut, where the radical Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine-General Command (PFLP-GC) has bases.
Lebanese security sources said no one was hurt.
The flare-up coincides with a renewed crisis between Israel and the Palestinians since two militant Islamic bombers killed themselves and 13 others in a Jerusalem market on July 30.
U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross is due in the region on Saturday on a mediation mission which Washington says will focus on Israeli insistence on enhanced security.
Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai, who was holding consultations with Israeli military commanders in the north, toured the damaged synagogue and told residents to "remain strong".
Speaking in English to reporters following the tour, Mordechai said:
"Hizbollah damaged today the agreement...We will do everything that we think that is necessary against the Hizbollah and other terrorism groups in Lebanon."
Hizbollah, which is fighting to drive Israeli troops from southern Lebanon, denied it had launched Friday's attack.

But the group's chief, Sheikh Hassan Nasrallah, told a news conference in Beirut that Hizbollah would resume Katyusha attacks on northern Israel because the 1996 accord had failed to protect Lebanese civilians.
"We say the resumption of using other means to protect civilians has become necessary," Nasrallah said. Hizbollah threatened earlier this week to carry out attacks inside Israel.

"The trouble here, the difficulty, is that the Hizbollah is continuing to act as a proxy army for the Syrians," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's aide David Bar-Illan told Reuters. Syria has 35,000 troops in Lebanon.
Israel set up the border zone in Lebanon with the declared aim of protecting its northern border.

It has halted peace talks with the PLO in response to the market bombings and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, stopping trade, preventing Palestinians from getting to jobs in Israel and freezing financial transfers.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat has slammed the blockade as a declaration of war and told Palestinians to "prepare for what will come".
His statement, and angry words from Netanyahu, drew a sharp rebuke on Thursday from U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright who urged both sides to revive a spirit of partnership on peace.
